stories.summary: Internal documents show a years-long Israeli program to upgrade Ugandan drone capability — surfacing exactly as Uganda prepares to send troops to a Gaza 'stabilization force'. Lead with the sequencing: the country being asked to police Gaza has been buying its aerial surveillance capacity from the state that besieged it. Who is affected — Ugandans under a government whose internal-security tooling is now foreign-supplied, and Palestinians who would be policed by it; who holds power — Elbit and the Israeli export authority that licenses these transfers, and Kampala, which paid. The structural why: arms-export relationships are how a state converts a client's troop commitment into a standing dependency, and the leak is the only reason any of it is public. Handle the documents carefully — describe what they show and what Drop Site verified. This is original documentary reporting, not a Washington claim; the value is the paper trail.

stories.label: Iran vows 'crushing' retaliation after latest US attacks
stories.summary: Iran's General Staff of the Armed Forces has promised 'crushing and devastating' blows after a new wave of US airstrikes on military positions in the southern provinces. Lead with what is verifiable and what is not, and say which is which — this is the Iranian state's own account of strikes on its own territory, and the feed carries no independent confirmation of the targets or the toll. Who is affected — residents of the southern provinces, and the Gulf shipping and energy corridor that prices every one of these exchanges; who holds power — the US command ordering the strikes and the General Staff choosing whether a threat becomes a launch. The structural why: this confrontation has moved into a phase where the contested ground is evidence itself, after last week's unverified Larak mine claim and the synthetic Kharg Island video. Attribute every casualty and target figure to Mehr explicitly. Iran is an OIC state and Mehr is the regional source; the feed offered no second outlet for this specific strike wave, so keep the sourcing caveat in the lead, not the footer.

stories.label: Zelenskyy Threatens to Shut Air Traffic Over Russia With Drones
stories.summary: Zelenskyy warned airlines off Russian airspace — 'there will simply be drones' — after escalating missile attacks on Ukrainian cities. Lead with the instrument, which is not the drone but the insurance underwriter: a state cannot legally close a rival's airspace, but a credible drone threat makes war-risk cover unpriceable, and the route closes itself. Who is affected — passengers and freight on the Europe-Asia corridors that already reroute around Ukraine, and Russian carriers whose foreign leases and reinsurance sit outside their government's reach; who holds power — Kyiv, which sets the threat level, and London and Bermuda reinsurers, who decide what it costs. The structural why: airspace denial by liability is the cheapest escalation available to the weaker air force, and it is reversible in a way a strike is not. This story carries the feed's second-highest sentiment divergence (0.32) — Bloomberg reports a warning, RT and Zero Hedge report a wild threat — so state the post's actual wording and let the reader judge.

stories.label: Apple Maps Renames Lake Ontario 'Lake America' After Trump Order
stories.summary: Apple followed Google in renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for US users, on a presidential order, while Canadian users still see Lake Ontario. Lead with the detail that makes it structural rather than absurd: the same lake now has two names depending on the SIM in your pocket, because both companies resolve place names against the user's jurisdiction. Who is affected — Canadians whose national geography was renamed by another state's executive order, and every reader who takes a map as a record of fact; who holds power — the two firms that operate the world's default geographic register and comply feature-by-feature. The structural why: geographic naming used to require a treaty or a war, and now requires an order and a per-country lookup table, which is a far cheaper instrument. Note the precedent this sets for contested names — Persian Gulf, Palestine, Kashmir — where the same switch already exists and can be flipped by whichever government asks. Say plainly that Lake Ontario has not been renamed by anyone with authority over it.

stories.label: John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
stories.summary: Apple's SEC filing puts the incoming CEO at about $58m for fiscal 2027 and the outgoing one at about $47m as executive chairman. Lead with the $47m: the number that is surprising is not the successor's pay but that stepping down costs roughly a fifth of the job. Who is affected — Apple shareholders and the contract manufacturers and app developers whose margins the new hardware-first CEO now sets; who holds power — a compensation committee pricing continuity, and Cook, whose chairman role keeps a vote in the room he just left. The structural why: an executive chairmanship at near-CEO pay is how a board buys against a succession it does not fully trust, and it is the detail that tells you how much authority actually transferred. Ternus is a hardware engineer taking over a company whose declared problem is AI — say what that choice signals. Public attention is real here: Ternus was among yesterday's most-read Wikipedia pages. Use the filing figures, not the estimates.

stories.label: Govt raises petrol price by Rs1.08, high-speed diesel by Rs0.51
stories.summary: Petrol goes to Rs343.87 and high-speed diesel to Rs370.92 a litre — but the number to lead with is Rs114, the per-litre tax and duty the state keeps regardless of the crude price. Who is affected — Pakistani households and the freight sector, where diesel is the input price under every food item in the country; who holds power — the finance ministry, which sets the levy, and the IMF programme conditions that make the levy the least-negotiable line in the budget. The structural why: when a third of the pump price is fiscal rather than commodity, a world oil rally and a domestic revenue target become indistinguishable to the person paying, and the state's incentive to pass through a price fall weakens. Set this against the Gulf-region energy disruption we covered this week, and show what share of the increase is crude and what share is policy. Pakistan is an OIC state and Dawn is the regional source and the originating reporter.

stories.label: PLD Space Adds €108 million to Series C Funding Round
stories.summary: A Spanish launch company extended its Series C to €288m, six months after closing it at €180m and before the Miura 5 rocket has flown once. Lead with that sequence: the round reopened on the strength of a maiden flight still ahead of it. Who is affected — European satellite operators currently buying rides from SpaceX or waiting on Ariane 6 slots, and Spanish public co-investors carrying the downside; who holds power — the investors pricing sovereign launch access as a strategic rather than a commercial asset. The structural why: Europe is capitalising launch capacity the way it capitalised chips, on security-of-supply logic, which means the valuation is not being set by the addressable market. Give the burn implied by €288m against a small-lift vehicle, and be clear what Miura 5 can and cannot lift — this is a payload class, not an Ariane competitor.

stories.label: Nepal-China Flood Deaths Top 1,000 as Rescuers Seek Survivors
stories.summary: More than 1,000 dead across Nepal and Tibet on the seventh day of rescue, from a glacial collapse that sent ice, rock and water down a single valley. Lead with the mechanism, because it is what makes this a science story and not a weather story: a glacial lake outburst flood arrives as a wall of debris in minutes, and the moraine dams holding these lakes were built by ice that is no longer there to maintain them. Who is affected — valley communities in Nepal and Tibet with no warning system between the lake and the settlement, and thousands still missing; who holds power — the governments that map these lakes and decide whether to fund siphoning, early-warning sensors, or nothing. The structural why: the Himalayan glacial lake inventory has grown for three decades and is documented, so the hazard was known and the failure is one of instrumentation, not of prediction. Give the elevation drop and the travel time if the reporting supports it — the number that explains why 1,000 people could not move.

stories.label: CDC reported then deleted two measles deaths that were questioned by RFK Jr.
stories.summary: The CDC removed two Pennsylvania measles deaths from its national count after the health secretary questioned them, publicly contradicting a state's own death determinations. Lead with the precedent being broken, not the politics: cause of death is certified by state and local officials, and federal surveillance has always aggregated those determinations rather than adjudicating them. Who is affected — every user of US mortality data, including the actuaries, journals and foreign health ministries that treat the CDC series as a baseline; who holds power — the secretary who raised the objection and the agency that acted on it. The structural why: a national statistical series is only usable if its inclusion rule is mechanical, and once deletions become discretionary the whole back-series loses its meaning, not just these two records. Name the two deaths as far as Pennsylvania's officials have described them, and state precisely what the CDC's stated justification was.

stories.label: China's 'Fire Ant' campaign used compromised Cisco routers as platform for more attacks
stories.summary: A campaign researchers call Fire Ant turned compromised Cisco routers into launch platforms — 'it compromised the trust layer those systems depend on', in the researchers' phrase. Lead with why a router is a different class of target than a server: it sits below the software that logs anything, terminates the tunnels, and is trusted by every device behind it, so a foothold there survives the reimaging of everything it serves. Who is affected — the network operators whose downstream customers were reached through their own edge hardware, without any of those customers being breached directly; who holds power — Cisco, whose firmware update path determines how long the hole stays open, and the operators who defer those updates because a router reboot is an outage. The structural why: network appliances have the longest patch latency and the weakest telemetry of anything in a datacentre, which is exactly why state groups have moved into them. Attribute the China attribution to the researchers and say what it rests on.

stories.label: Meta's $17 billion teen safety settlement could change social media, but who gets a say?
stories.summary: Fifty-two US state attorneys general settled with Meta for $17bn over teen safety — and SMEX, writing from Beirut, asks the question the US coverage does not: the product changes bought by that settlement will ship globally, negotiated by parties representing none of the users outside the United States. Lead with the asymmetry in a number, not a grievance: the share of Meta's users covered by the settling jurisdictions against the share who will get the resulting defaults. Who is affected — teenagers in the Arab world and the global South, where the same age-assurance and content defaults arrive without the local consultation, legal recourse, or Arabic-language moderation capacity that would make them work; who holds power — the AGs, and Meta, which prefers one global product spec. The structural why: a US settlement is now a de facto global regulation because compliance is cheaper to implement once, which makes American state litigation the world's most consequential unelected standards body. Connect to the Punjab under-16 resolution we covered — same age-verification architecture, opposite direction of authority.

stories.label: 'Extraction without compensation' - the AI dilemma facing SA's digital media
stories.summary: A new report, 'The Protocol Gap: South Africa', finds South African publishers facing a choice with no good branch: block the AI crawlers and lose search visibility, or allow them and be summarised out of a business model. Lead with the protocol itself — robots.txt is a request, not a control, and the same file governs the crawler that sends you readers and the one that replaces you. Who is affected — South African newsrooms with no licensing leverage and no domestic AI firm to negotiate with; who holds power — Google, which fused the two crawlers' incentives by putting summaries above the links, and the publishers whose only instrument is a text file honoured voluntarily. The structural why: the licensing deals struck by large Northern publishers work precisely because those publishers can credibly withhold, and a market of small national outlets cannot — so the same technology produces payment in one place and extraction in another. Give the report's own findings on how many SA publishers actually block. Africa dateline; this is the continent's version of a fight that has so far been reported from New York and London.
